verses.zh: 耶稣进了耶利哥，正经过的时候，
verses.en: Jesus[NOTE:1] entered Jericho[NOTE:2] and was passing through it.
notes: Grk “And entering, he passed through”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity. Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
For location see Map5-B2; Map6-E1; Map7-E1; Map8-E3; Map10-A2; Map11-A1.
verses.commentary:
19:1 "Jericho" Jericho is one of the most ancient cities in the ANE. It is located about nineteen miles
northeast of Jerusalem on the western side of the Jordan River close to the mouth of the Dead Sea. It was noted
for its balsam wood and date palms (cf. Josephus, Antiq. 15.4.2). It was once Anthony's gift to Cleopatra.
There were apparently an old town and a new town, which helped explain the apparent discrepancy in the Synoptics
between "entering" (Luke 18:35; 19:1) and "leaving" (Matt. 20:29; Mark 10:46).

▣ "was passing through" Luke uses this term often. It is a compound of dia and erchomai.
Here it is an IMPERFECT MIDDLE (deponent) INDICATIVE, which denotes the beginning
of an action. This same TENSE can emphasize repeated action in past time, but this meaning does
not make sense in this context. Context, not lexicons or Greek grammar, is the key to authorial intent.
Words and forms have meaning only in a specific literary context.

Here are some examples of how Luke uses this term.

- "to proceed," Luke 2:15 (cf. Acts 9:38)

- "to pierce through," Luke 3:35

- "to pass through," Luke 4:30

- "to spread abroad a rumor," Luke 5:15

- "to pass over," Luke 8:22

- "to pass along," Luke 9:4

- "to travel through a country," Luke 9:6

verses.zh: 有一个人名叫撒该，作税吏长，是个财主。
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] a man named Zacchaeus was there; he was a chief tax collector[NOTE:2] and was rich.
notes: Grk “And behold.” Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the introduction of a new character. The Greek word ἰδού (idou) at the beginning of this statement has not been translated because it has no exact English equivalent here, but adds interest and emphasis (BDAG 468 s.v. 1).

This is the one place in the NT the office of chief tax collector is noted. If the term refers to a managerial rank, this individual would organize and oversee the other tax collectors and collect significant commissions (see also the note on the word tax collector in 3:12). It is possible, however, that in this context the term simply means “major tax collector” and is a comment on the individual’s importance or wealth rather than his rank (see D. L. Bock, Luke [BECNT] 1:1516).
verses.commentary:
19:2 "Zaccheus" This is a Hebrew term meaning "pure" or "innocent" (cf. BDB 269). He will fulfill his name
in this encounter with Jesus.

▣ "he was a chief tax collector" The term architelōnēs is very unusual and is not
found in the Septuagint, Koine Papyri, or Greek literature, but it seems to mean that he was a tax commissioner
over the district of Jericho. He would have purchased this position from the Roman authorities. The local Jews
hated and ostracized those who worked for Rome because they often, if not always, overtaxed them. This is how
they made their salaries.

▣ "and he was rich" Although he had wealth, he was not happy. He seems to be a perfect example of
the truth found in Luke 18:24-27. Zaccheus is a literary foil to the rich, young ruler of Luke 18.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

verses.zh: 他要看看耶稣是怎样的人；只因人多，他的身量又矮，所以不得看见，
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] was trying to get a look at Jesus,[NOTE:2] but being a short man he could not see over the crowd.[NOTE:3]
notes: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “He was trying to see who Jesus was.”
Grk “and he was not able to because of the crowd, for he was short in stature.”
verses.commentary:
19:3 "was trying to see who Jesus was" This IMPERFECT TENSE here means continual action in
past time. The Holy Spirit had already done His work (cf, John 16:8-15) drawing this man.

▣ "for he was small in stature" This term usually means "age" (cf. Luke 2:52; John 9:21,23; Heb. 11:11),
but in the NT it can also mean "height" (cf. Luke 12:25; and possibly 2:52 and Eph. 4:13; Matt. 6:27). In this
context the phrase can refer to the height or stature of Zaccheus or Jesus, but most probably of Zaccheus.

Modern anthropology informs us that most men of this time period and locale were about
5'5". Therefore, Zaccheus must have been noticibly shorter than this.

verses.zh: 就跑到前头，爬上桑树，要看耶稣，因为耶稣必从那里经过。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree[NOTE:2] to see him because Jesus[NOTE:3] was going to pass that way.
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of Zacchaeus not being able to see over the crowd.
A sycamore tree would have large branches near the ground like an oak tree and would be fairly easy to climb. These trees reach a height of some 50 ft (about 15 m).
Grk “that one”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
19:4 "he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree" This is highly unusual for an Oriental of great
wealth. His pride was gone. He had heard that Jesus accepted and fellowshipped with tax collectors. One was
even one of His close associates (i.e., Levi, also known as Matthew).

▣ "sycamore" This is not the same as the sycamore tree in America. This tree is of the nettle family,
which also includes the mulberry and fig. In Greek the term sukomorea is made up of "fig" (sukon)
and "mulberry" (moron). It was a large tree with low branches, which made it easy to climb (cf. United
Bible Societies, Fauna and Flora of the Bible, pp. 179-182).

verses.zh: 耶稣到了那里，抬头一看，对他说：「撒该，快下来！今天我必住在你家里。」
verses.en: And when Jesus came to that place, he looked up[NOTE:1] and said to him, “Zacchaeus, come down quickly[NOTE:2] because I must[NOTE:3] stay at your house today.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Most mss (A [D] W [Ψ] ƒ13 33vid M latt) read “Jesus looking up, saw him and said.” The words “saw him and” are not in א B L T Θ ƒ1 579 1241 2542 co. Both the testimony for the omission and the natural tendency toward scribal expansion argue for the shorter reading here.
Grk “hastening, come down.” σπεύσας (speusas) has been translated as a participle of manner.
I must stay. Jesus revealed the necessity of his associating with people like Zacchaeus (5:31-32). This act of fellowship indicated acceptance.
On today here and in v. 9, see the note on today in 2:11.
verses.commentary:
19:5 "He looked up and said to him, 'Zaccheus, hurry and come down’" This is an AORIST ACTIVE
PARTICIPLE (used in the sense of an IMPERATIVE) combined with an AORIST ACTIVE
IMPERATIVE which means "come down quickly." I wonder how Jesus knew his name. Some commentators use
John 1:47-48 as a parallel of Jesus' supernatural knowledge.

▣ "I must stay at your house" Jesus had a divine appointment with this man (use of dei). I am
so glad Jesus loved outcasts, both rich and poor, male and female, slave and free, Jew and Gentile (cf. Gal. 3:28; Col. 3:11)!

verses.zh: 他就急忙下来，欢欢喜喜地接待耶稣。
verses.en: So he came down quickly[NOTE:1] and welcomed Jesus[NOTE:2] joyfully.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “hastening, he came down.” σπεύσας (speusas) has been translated as a participle of manner.
Grk “him”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The participle χαίρων (chairōn) has been taken as indicating manner.sn Zacchaeus responded joyfully. Luke likes to mention joy as a response to what God was doing (1:14; 2:10; 10:20; 13:17; 15:5, 32; 19:37; 24:41, 52).

verses.zh: 众人看见，都私下议论说：「他竟到罪人家里去住宿。」
verses.en: And when the people[NOTE:1] saw it, they all complained,[NOTE:2] “He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “they”; the referent is unspecified but is probably the crowd in general, who would have no great love for a man like Zacchaeus who had enriched himself many times over at their expense.

This term is used only twice in the NT, both times in Luke (here and 15:2) and has negative connotations both times (BDAG 227 s.v. διαγογγύζω). The participle λέγοντες (legontes) is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
Being the guest of a man who is a sinner was a common complaint about Jesus: Luke 5:31-32; 7:37-50; 15:1-2.
verses.commentary:
19:7 "When they saw it, they all began to grumble" This is another IMPERFECT TENSE. The
root word for "grumble" is from the buzzing of bees (cf. Luke 5:30). It was used in the Septuagint to describe
the griping (murmuring) of Israel (cf. Exod. 15:24; 16:2,7,8; Num. 14:2). It is found only twice in the NT,
both in Luke's Gospel (cf. Luke 15:2; 19:7). The local Jews felt that Jesus' fellowship with sinners (those
unable or unwilling to observe the Oral Traditions) made him ceremonially unclean and theologically suspect
(i.e., 5:30-32; 7:37-50; 15:1-2).

verses.zh: 撒该站着对主说：「主啊，我把所有的一半给穷人；我若讹诈了谁，就还他四倍。」
verses.en: But Zacchaeus stopped and said to the Lord, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I now give[NOTE:1] to the poor, and if[NOTE:2] I have cheated anyone of anything, I am paying back four times as much!”
notes: Zacchaeus was a penitent man who resolved on the spot to act differently in the face of Jesus’ acceptance of him. In resolving to give half his possessions to the poor, Zacchaeus was not defending himself against the crowd’s charges and claiming to be righteous. Rather as a result of this meeting with Jesus, he was a changed individual. So Jesus could speak of salvation coming that day (v. 9) and of the lost being saved (v. 10).
This is a first class condition in the Greek text. It virtually confesses fraud.
verses.commentary:
19:8 "Zaccheus stopped and said" Zaccheus must have heard the murmuring! This is his public statement of
confession, repentance, and restitution as a sign that a brand new relationship of love and forgiveness had
been established with God through this encounter with Jesus, the Messiah.

▣ "half of my possessions I will give to the poor" This was a large amount of money. Being right
with God opens one's eyes to the needs of the poor!

Some think this refers to his regular actions, like Cornelius (cf. Acts 10:2), but in context
it seems that it refers to his accumulated wealth. This man is an antithesis to the rich man in Luke 18.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALMSGIVING

▣ "if" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE, which is assumed to be true. He
was publicly admitting that he had defrauded the people.

▣ "I will give back four times as much" He was using the OT standard from Exod. 22:1 and the example
in 2 Sam. 12:6 as restitution for a violent robbery. This was a much larger sum than Lev. 6:5 and Num. 5:7
required, where only an added one fifth was required as restitution. His restitution was a proof of a changed
heart, not a means to it. This statement, combined with the previous promise, meant he was not a wealthy man
anymore. What a contrast to Luke 18!

verses.zh: 耶稣说：「今天救恩到了这家，因为他也是亚伯拉罕的子孙。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] Jesus said to him, “Today salvation[NOTE:2] has come to this household[NOTE:3] because he too is a son of Abraham![NOTE:4]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative
This is one of the few uses of the specific term salvation in Luke (1:69, 71, 77), though the concept runs throughout the Gospel.
The household is not a reference to the building, but to the people who lived within it (L&N 10.8).
Zacchaeus was personally affirmed by Jesus as a descendant (son) of Abraham and a member of God’s family.
verses.commentary:
19:9 "And Jesus said to him, 'Today salvation has come to this house'" A new relationship with God was
evidenced by this man's changed attitude and actions, which impacted his whole family (cf. Acts 10:2; 11:14;
16:15,31-33; 18:8). This salvation was a present reality (cf. 2 Cor. 6:2), as well as a future consummation.

The phrase "to this house" implies that the other members of the extended family and servants
would be affected by Zaccheus' conversion. Household evangelism is seen several times in Acts (cf. Acts 10:2;
11:14; 16:15,31-34; 18:8). Western individualism is not the only biblical model.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOUSEHOLD BAPTISMS

▣ "because he, too, is a son of Abraham" Apparently he was already a racial Jew, but now through
faith in Jesus, he had become a true descendant of Abraham by faith (cf. Rom. 2:28-29; 3:22; 4:11-12; 10:12;
Gal. 3:9,26,28,29; 4:5,12; 5:6; 6:15). His lineage did not bring salvation, but his faith, evidenced by his
public confession and restitution, surely did!

verses.zh: 人子来，为要寻找、拯救失丧的人。」
verses.en: For the Son of Man came[NOTE:1] to seek and to save the lost.”
notes: The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost is Jesus’ mission succinctly defined. See Luke 15:1-32.
verses.commentary:
19:10 "the Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost" This may be an allusion to the
Septuagint of Ezek. 34:16 and it certainly relates to Luke 1:68-79. It is the theological emphasis of Luke 15's
parables. It is also similar to the central summary statement of the Gospel of Mark (cf. Mark 10:45 and 1 Tim. 1:15).
Theologically Jesus came for several reasons:

- to reveal the Father

- to die for sin

- to give converted humans an example to follow

In this context the redemptive theme is emphasized. Both VERBALS "seek" and "save"
are AORIST ACTIVE INFINITIVES.

The word "lost" is a PERFECT ACTIVE PARTICIPLE of apollumi, which means
to destroy. Here it is used as imagery for permanent spiritual loss (see Matt. 10:6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: DESTRUCTION
(apollumi)

verses.zh: 众人正在听见这些话的时候，耶稣因为将近耶路撒冷，又因他们以为　神的国快要显出来，就另设一个比喻，说：
verses.en: While the people were listening to these things, Jesus[NOTE:1] proceeded to tell a parable because he was near to Jerusalem,[NOTE:2] and because they thought[NOTE:3] that the kingdom of God[NOTE:4] was going to[NOTE:5] appear immediately.
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
The present active infinitive δοκεῖν (dokein) has been translated as causal.
Luke means here the appearance of the full kingdom of God in power with the Son of Man as judge as Luke 17:22-37 describes.
Or perhaps, “the kingdom of God must appear immediately (see L&N 71.36).
verses.commentary:
19:11 "a parable" See the Introduction to Luke 8, Contextual Insights, B., for the hermeneutical principles
for interpreting parables.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERPRETING PARABLES

▣ Jesus gives two reasons for telling this parable at this time and place:

- He was approaching Jerusalem

- the crowd was expecting an immediate coming of the Kingdom

Many commentators assert that Luke's Gospel accentuates a delayed Second Coming. This parable is
one evidence (cf. Robert H. Stein, The Method and Message of Jesus' Teachings, pp. 54-55).

SPECIAL TOPIC: DELAYED SECOND COMING

▣ "the kingdom of God was going to appear immediately" The Jews only expected one climactic
coming of God in history through the Messiah and the setting up of the Age of Righteousness with Jews in
charge! Many thought this would happen when Jesus came to Jerusalem at Passover.

The time frame ("immediately") relates to Mal. 3:1.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KINGDOM OF GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: SOON RETURN

verses.zh: 「有一个贵胄往远方去，要得国回来，
verses.en: Therefore he said, “A nobleman[NOTE:1] went to a distant country to receive[NOTE:2] for himself a kingdom and then return.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “a man of noble birth” or “a man of noble status” (L&N 87.27).

Note that the receiving of the kingdom takes place in the far country. This suggests that those in the far country recognize and acknowledge the king when his own citizens did not want him as king (v. 14; cf. John 1:11-12).

The background to this story about the nobleman who went…to receive for himself a kingdom had some parallels in the area’s recent history: Archelaus was appointed ethnarch of Judea, Samaria, and Idumea in 4 b.c., but the people did not like him. Herod the Great also made a similar journey to Rome where he was crowned King of Judea in 40 b.c., although he was not able to claim his kingdom until 37 b.c.
verses.commentary:
19:12 This is similar to Matt. 25:14-30. Obviously Jesus used the same themes and teachings in different
settings for different purposes.

NASB, NRSV, NJB
"a nobleman"

NKJV
"a certain nobleman"

TEV
"there was once a man"

REB
"a man of noble birth"

Peshitta
"a great man of a noble family"

This parable is introduced with tis, which is normally translated "a certain." Many of
Luke's parables are introduced with this textual marker (cf. Luke 7:41; 10:30; 14:16; 15:11; 16:1,19; 19:12).

▣ "A nobleman went to a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself, and then return" Many
historians see this as an allusion to Herod the Great's death and his son Archelaus's attempted succession
(cf. Luke 19:14, which is an unusual footnote). This historical incident is recorded in
Josephus' Antiq. 17.

verses.zh: 便叫了他的十个仆人来，交给他们十锭（锭：原文是弥拿，一弥拿约银十两）银子，说：『你们去做生意，直等我回来。』
verses.en: And he summoned ten of his slaves,[NOTE:1] gave them ten minas,[NOTE:2] and said to them, ‘Do business with these until I come back.’
notes: See the note on the word “slave” in 7:2.
That is, one for each. A mina was a Greek monetary unit worth 100 denarii or about four months’ wages for an average worker based on a six-day work week.
verses.commentary:
19:13 "he called ten of his slaves" Although he called ten, only three are mentioned specifically. The
term doulos would denote a household servant.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS
IN SCRIPTURE, #5

▣ "and gave them ten minas" This is the Greek term maneh (Semitic loan word mena),
which equals one hundred drachmas, (one sixth of a talent). A drachma is equivalent to
a denarius, which was the day's wage for a laborer or soldier. Therefore, this was less than one third
of a year's wage, not a large sum at all. It may reflect this master's stinginess or frugality.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COINS USED IN
PALESTINE IN JESUS' DAY

NASB, NRSV
"do business with this until I come back"

NKJV
"do business till I come"

TEV
"See what you can earn with this while I am gone"

NJB
"Trade with these, until I get back"

REB
"Trade with this while I am away"

Peshitta
"Transact business until I come back"

This is an AORIST MIDDLE (deponent) IMPERTIVE ("do business")
followed by a PRESENT MIDDLE (deponent) INDICATIVE ("while I am gone"). In
John 14:3 it is used of the return of Jesus. The master was testing the skills and trustworthiness of his servants.
He gave them some responsibility! He will call them to account at an unspecified future date (cf. Luke 19:15-20).

verses.zh: 他本国的人却恨他，打发使者随后去，说：『我们不愿意这个人作我们的王。』
verses.en: But his citizens[NOTE:1] hated[NOTE:2] him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man[NOTE:3] to be king[NOTE:4] over us!’
notes: Or “subjects.” Technically these people were not his subjects yet, but would be upon his return. They were citizens of his country who opposed his appointment as their king; later the newly-appointed king will refer to them as his “enemies” (v. 27).
The imperfect is intense in this context, suggesting an ongoing attitude.
Grk “this one” (somewhat derogatory in this context).
Or “to rule.”

verses.zh: 他既得国回来，就吩咐叫那领银子的仆人来，要知道他们做生意赚了多少。
verses.en: When[NOTE:1] he returned after receiving the kingdom, he summoned[NOTE:2] these slaves to whom he had given the money. He wanted[NOTE:3] to know how much they had earned[NOTE:4] by trading.
notes: Grk “And it happened that when.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
Grk “he said for these slaves to be called to him.” The passive construction has been translated as an active one and simplified to “he summoned.”

Grk “in order that he might know” (a continuation of the preceding sentence). Due to the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was started here in the translation by supplying the pronoun “he” as subject and the verb “wanted” to convey the idea of purpose.
The Greek verb earned refers to profit from engaging in commerce and trade (L&N 57.195). This is an examination of stewardship.

verses.zh: 头一个上来，说：『主啊，你的一锭银子已经赚了十锭。』
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] the first one came before him and said, ‘Sir,[NOTE:2] your mina[NOTE:3] has made ten minas more.’
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of the royal summons.
Or “Lord”; or “Master.” (and so throughout this paragraph).
See the note on the word “minas” in v. 13.

verses.zh: 主人说：『好！良善的仆人，你既在最小的事上有忠心，可以有权柄管十座城。』
verses.en: And the king[NOTE:1] said to him, ‘Well done, good slave! Because you have been faithful[NOTE:2] in a very small matter, you will have authority[NOTE:3] over ten cities.’
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (the nobleman of v. 12, now a king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
See Luke 16:10.
The faithful slave received expanded responsibility (authority over ten cities) as a result of his faithfulness; this in turn is an exhortation to faithfulness for the reader.
verses.commentary:
19:17

NASB
"you are to be in authority over ten cities"

NKJV
"have authority over ten cities"

NRSV
"take charge of ten cities"

TEV, REB
"I will put you in charge of ten cities"

NJB
"you shall have the government of ten cities"

Peshitta
"you will have charge over ten talents"

This is a PERIPHRASTIC PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE, which denotes continuing
authority.

The Aramaic word "talent" in the Peshitta is very similar to the word city.

- Aramaic ‒ kakra/"talent"

- Aramaic ‒ karkha/"city"

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEGREES OF REWARDS AND PUNISHMENT

verses.zh: 第二个来，说：『主啊，你的一锭银子已经赚了五锭。』
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] the second one came and said, ‘Sir, your mina has made five minas.’
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.

verses.zh: 主人说：『你也可以管五座城。』
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] the king[NOTE:2] said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of the second slave’s report.
Grk “he”; the referent (the nobleman of v. 12, now a king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 又有一个来说：『主啊，看哪，你的一锭银子在这里，我把它包在手巾里存着。
verses.en: Then another[NOTE:1] slave[NOTE:2] came and said, ‘Sir, here is[NOTE:3] your mina that I put away for safekeeping[NOTE:4] in a piece of cloth.[NOTE:5]
notes: Though ten were given minas, the story stops to focus on the one who did nothing with the opportunity given to him. Here is the parable’s warning about the one who does not trust the master. This figure is called “another,” marking him out as different than the first two.
The word “slave” is not in the Greek text, but has been supplied for stylistic reasons.
Grk “behold.”
Or “that I stored away.” L&N 85.53 defines ἀπόκειμαι (apokeimai) here as “to put something away for safekeeping—‘to store, to put away in a safe place.’”
The piece of cloth, called a σουδάριον (soudarion), could have been a towel, napkin, handkerchief, or face cloth (L&N 6.159).
verses.commentary:
19:20 "handkerchief" Possibly there is an Aramaic confusion between the word "ground" (see parallel in
Matt. 25:25) and "handkerchief." The custom of the day would have this man burying the money in the ground for
safekeeping. However, this term is used of a cloth in John 11:44.

verses.zh: 我原是怕你，因为你是严厉的人；没有放下的，还要去拿，没有种下的，还要去收。』
verses.en: For I was afraid of you because you are a severe[NOTE:1] man. You withdraw[NOTE:2] what you did not deposit[NOTE:3] and reap what you did not sow.’
notes: Or “exacting,” “harsh,” “hard.”

Grk “man, taking out.” The Greek word can refer to withdrawing money from a bank (L&N 57.218), and in this context of financial accountability that is the most probable meaning. Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was started here in the translation by supplying the pronoun “you” as subject and translating the participle αἴρεις (aireis) as a finite verb.
The Greek verb τίθημι (tithēmi) can be used of depositing money with a banker to earn interest (L&N 57.217). In effect the slave charges that the master takes what he has not earned.
verses.commentary:
19:21 "I was afraid of you" This is an IMPERFECT MIDDLE (deponent) INDICATIVE,
which denotes repeated action in past time. Paralyzing fear is not a motive for effective service.

NASB, NJB
"you are an exacting man"

NKJV
"you are an austere man"

NRSV, Peshitta
"you are a harsh man"

TEV, REB
"you are a hard man"

This Greek word is used in the Septuagint of II Macc. 14:30 for "harsh," "rough," or
"sour behavior." It is used in the Koine Papyri for an exacting, strict, penny-pincher and letter-of-the-law
type of personality.

This word is just part of the parable. It in no way describes Christ at judgment (cf. 2 Cor. 5:10).

verses.zh: 主人对他说：『你这恶仆，我要凭你的口定你的罪。你既知道我是严厉的人，没有放下的，还要去拿，没有种下的，还要去收，
verses.en: The king[NOTE:1] said to him, ‘I will judge you by your own words,[NOTE:2] you wicked slave![NOTE:3] So you knew, did you, that I was a severe[NOTE:4] man, withdrawing what I didn’t deposit and reaping what I didn’t sow?
notes: Grk “He”; the referent (the nobleman of v. 12, now a king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “out of your own mouth” (an idiom).
Note the contrast between this slave, described as “wicked,” and the slave in v. 17, described as “good.”
Or “exacting,” “harsh,” “hard.”
verses.commentary:
19:22 Some translations make this verse a question (NASB, NRSV, NJB, NIV), but others see it as an
affirmation (NKJV, TEV, NAB).

verses.zh: 为甚么不把我的银子交给银行，等我来的时候，连本带利都可以要回来呢？』
verses.en: Why then didn’t you put[NOTE:1] my money in the bank,[NOTE:2] so that when I returned I could have collected it with interest?’
notes: That is, “If you really feared me why did you not do a minimum to get what I asked for?”
Grk “on the table”; the idiom refers to a place where money is kept or managed, or credit is established, thus “bank” (L&N 57.215).

verses.zh: 就对旁边站着的人说：『夺过他这一锭来，给那有十锭的。』
verses.en: And he said to his attendants,[NOTE:1] ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has ten.’[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “to those standing by,” but in this context involving an audience before the king to give an accounting, these would not be casual bystanders but courtiers or attendants.
Grk “the ten minas.”
verses.commentary:
19:24-26 Remember this is a Near Eastern parable, which often uses hyperbole. The details of the story
cannot be allegorized. These overstatements are usually part of the surprising twist which denotes the main
point of the parable. Possibly this is analogous to Luke 8:18.

The central paradox of the gospel is that salvation is free in the finished work of the Messiah,
but the resulting reality is a cost-everything service (cf. Eph. 2:8-9,10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEGREES OF REWARDS AND PUNISHMENT

verses.zh: 他们说：『主啊，他已经有十锭了。』
verses.en: But[NOTE:1] they said to him, ‘Sir, he has ten minas already!’[NOTE:2]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast present in this context. Those watching the evaluation are shocked, as the one with the most gets even more. The word “already” is supplied at the end of the statement to indicate this surprise and shock.
A few mss (D W 69 and a few versional witnesses) omit this verse either to harmonize it with Matt 25:28-29 or to keep the king’s speech seamless.
verses.commentary:
19:25 The NKJV and NRSV put this verse in brackets because some ancient Greek texts omit it (MSS D, W,
several lectionaries, as well as some Old Latin, Syrian, and Coptic translations. The UBS4 translation
committee rates its inclusion as "A" (certain)!

verses.zh: 主人说：『我告诉你们，凡有的，还要加给他；没有的，连他所有的也要夺过来。
verses.en: ‘I tell you that everyone who has will be given more,[NOTE:1] but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “to everyone who has, he will be given more.” sn Everyone who has will be given more. Again, faithfulness yields great reward (see Luke 8:18; also Matt 13:12; Mark 4:25).

The one who has nothing has even what he seems to have taken away from him, ending up with no reward at all (see also Luke 8:18). The exact force of this is left ambiguous, but there is no comfort here for those who are pictured by the third slave as being totally unmoved by the master. Though not an outright enemy, there is no relationship to the master either. Three groups are represented in the parable: the faithful of various sorts (vv. 16, 18); the unfaithful who associate with Jesus but do not trust him (v. 21); and the enemies (v. 27).
verses.commentary:
19:26 One wonders how far to push the details of this (and every) parable. Is it possible to identify

- the nobleman as Jesus (Luke 19:12)

- the slaves (Luke 19:13) as disciples

- the citizens (Luke 19:14) as Israel or the people living in Jerusalem

If so then Luke 19:26 presents the interesting question, "Is the slave punished but still in the
family (cf. Luke 8:18; Matt. 13:12; 25:29; Mark 4:25; 1 Cor. 3:10-15; Jude 23)? The Parable of the Soils
(Matthew 13; Mark 4; Luke 8) strongly suggests that some initially respond, but do not remain.

Although the speculation is interesting, usually parables have one main truth or at least one
truth connected to each main character. Often the details are just part of the story. See Introduction to Luke 8.

(aphistēmi)

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERPRETING PARABLES

verses.zh: 至于我那些仇敌，不要我作他们王的，把他们拉来，在我面前杀了吧！』」
verses.en: But as for these enemies of mine who did not want me to be their king,[NOTE:1] bring them here and slaughter[NOTE:2] them[NOTE:3] in front of me!’”
notes: Grk “to rule over them.”
This term, when used of people rather than animals, has some connotations of violence and mercilessness (L&N 20.72).
Slaughter them. To reject the king is to face certain judgment from him.
verses.commentary:
19:27 "But bring these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slay
them in my presence" This statement refers to Luke 19:14. Exactly how the people who rejected the master's
reign relate to the slave who did not act, is uncertain. Possibly two groups are judged:

- those who reject the master's reign

- those who refuse to act in the service of the master

The introduction in Luke 19:11 relates this to Jesus' triumphal entry into Jerusalem. The people
and their leaders will reject Jesus and be rejected for different reasons, related to #1. Zaccheus was fully
accepted and his actions proved it.

verses.zh: 耶稣说完了这话，就在前面走，上耶路撒冷去。
verses.en: After Jesus[NOTE:1] had said this, he continued on ahead,[NOTE:2] going up to Jerusalem.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
This could mean “before [his disciples],” but that is slightly more awkward, requiring an elided element (the disciples) to be supplied.

For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.sn This is yet another travel note on the journey to Jerusalem. See also Luke 18:31; 19:11. Jesus does not actually enter Jerusalem until 19:45.
verses.commentary:
19:28 This paragraph division matches NRSV. This continues Luke's theme of Jesus' travels to Jerusalem,
begun in Luke 9:51 and here concluded in His triumphal entry.

verses.zh: 将近伯法其和伯大尼，在一座山名叫橄榄山那里，就打发两个门徒，说：
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] when he approached Bethphage[NOTE:2] and Bethany, at the place called the Mount of Olives,[NOTE:3] he sent two of the disciples,
notes: Grk “And it happened that when.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated. Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the transition to a new topic.
The exact location of the village of Bethphage is not known. Most locate it on the southeast side of the Mount of Olives and northwest of Bethany, about 1.5 miles (3 km) east of Jerusalem.

Grk “at the mountain called ‘of Olives.’” This form of reference is awkward in contemporary English, so the more familiar “Mount of Olives” has been used in the translation.sn “Mountain” in English generally denotes a higher elevation than it often does in reference to places in Palestine. The Mount of Olives is really a ridge running north to south about 1.8 mi (3 km) long, east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley. Its central elevation is about 100 ft (30 m) higher than Jerusalem. It was named for the large number of olive trees which grew on it.
verses.commentary:
19:29 "Bethphage" The Talmud says this was a suburb of Jerusalem. The exact location is uncertain. Its
name meant "house of unripened figs" (cf. Matt. 21:1; Mark 11:1).

▣ "Bethany" This name means "house of dates" (cf. Matt. 21:17; Mark 11:1). This village was about
two miles away from Jerusalem on the opposite side of the ridge of which the Mount of Olives was a part. When
Jesus was in Jerusalem, He normally stayed in the home of Mary, Martha, and Lazarus, which was located in Bethany.

verses.zh: 「你们往对面村子里去，进去的时候，必看见一匹驴驹拴在那里，是从来没有人骑过的，可以解开牵来。
verses.en: telling them,[NOTE:1] “Go to the village ahead of you.[NOTE:2] When[NOTE:3] you enter it, you will find a colt tied there that has never been ridden.[NOTE:4] Untie it and bring it here.
notes: Grk “saying.”
Grk “the village lying before [you]” (BDAG 530 s.v. κατέναντι 2.a).
Grk “in which entering.” This is a continuation of the previous sentence in Greek, but because of the length and complexity of the construction a new sentence was started here in the translation.
Grk “a colt tied there on which no one of men has ever sat.”
verses.commentary:
19:30 "you will find a colt tied on which no one yet has ever sat" This is a prophetic (typological)
fulfillment of Zech. 9:9 (cf. Matt. 21:2). It must be remembered that the donkey (mule, cf. 2 Sam. 18:9;
1 Kgs. 1:33) was a royal mount of the kings of Israel. Near eastern asses were large, stately animals
(United Bible Societies, Fauna and Flora of the Bible, 2nd ed., pp. 5-7). This was a
symbol of Jesus' kingliness, not simply His being a man of peace. The reason it was a colt that no one
had ridden is because the king had his own donkey that no one else rode (cf. 1 Kgs. 1:33). Jesus had either
made previous arrangements (cf. Luke 19:31, 33-34) for this animal or he was using His supernatural knowledge.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TYPOLOGY

verses.zh: 若有人问为甚么解它，你们就说：『主要用它。』」
verses.en: If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ just say, ‘The Lord needs[NOTE:1] it.’”
notes: The custom called angaria allowed the impressment of animals for service to a significant figure.
verses.commentary: 19:31 "if" This is a THIRD CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE, which denotes potential action.

verses.zh: 打发的人去了，所遇见的正如耶稣所说的。
verses.en: So those who were sent ahead found[NOTE:1] it exactly[NOTE:2] as he had told them.
notes: Grk “sent ahead and went and found.”
Exactly as he had told them. Nothing in Luke 19-23 catches Jesus by surprise. Often he directs the action.

verses.zh: 他们解驴驹的时候，主人问他们说：「解驴驹做甚么？」
verses.en: As[NOTE:1] they were untying the colt, its owners asked them,[NOTE:2] “Why are you untying that colt?”
notes: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “said to them.”

verses.zh: 他们说：「主要用它。」
verses.en: They replied, “The Lord needs it.”

verses.zh: 他们牵到耶稣那里，把自己的衣服搭在上面，扶着耶稣骑上。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] they brought it to Jesus, threw their cloaks[NOTE:2] on the colt,[NOTE:3] and had Jesus get on[NOTE:4] it.
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “garments,” but this refers in context to their outer cloaks. The action is like 2 Kgs 9:13.
See Zech 9:9.

Although ἐπεβίβασαν (epebibasan) is frequently translated “set [Jesus] on it” or “put [Jesus] on it,” when used of a riding animal the verb can mean “to cause to mount” (L&N 15.98); thus here “had Jesus get on it.” The degree of assistance is not specified.

verses.zh: 走的时候，众人把衣服铺在路上。
verses.en: As[NOTE:1] he rode along, they[NOTE:2] spread their cloaks on the road.
notes: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.

The disciples initiated this action (since in 19:35 and 37 they are the subject) but the other gospels indicate the crowds also became involved. Thus it is difficult to specify the referent here as “the disciples” or “people.”
verses.commentary:
19:36 "they were spreading their coats on the road" This was a sign of kingship (cf. 2 Kgs. 9:13). Luke
does not mention the palm branches here. This event is characterizes as "the triumphal entry into Jerusalem"
(cf. Matt. 21:1-9; Mark 11:1-10; John 12:12-15).

verses.zh: 将近耶路撒冷，正下橄榄山的时候，众门徒因所见过的一切异能，都欢乐起来，大声赞美　神，
verses.en: As he approached the road leading down from[NOTE:1] the Mount of Olives,[NOTE:2] the whole crowd of his[NOTE:3] disciples began to rejoice[NOTE:4] and praise[NOTE:5] God with a loud voice for all the mighty works[NOTE:6] they had seen:[NOTE:7]
notes: Grk “the descent of”; this could refer to either the slope of the hillside itself or the path leading down from it (the second option has been adopted for the translation, see L&N 15.109).
See the note on the name Mount of Olives in v. 29.
Grk “the”; the Greek article has been translated here as a possessive pronoun (ExSyn 215).
Here the participle χαίροντες (chairontes) has been translated as a finite verb in English; it could also be translated adverbially as a participle of manner: “began to praise God joyfully.”
Or “works of power,” “miracles.” Jesus’ ministry of miracles is what has drawn attention. See Luke 7:22.
Grk “they had seen, saying.” The participle λέγοντες (legontes) is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
verses.commentary:
19:37 "near the descent of the Mount of Olives" M. R. Vincent, Word Studies, vol. 1, p. 208, makes
the topological comment that on this pilgrim road approaching Jerusalem one can see the city briefly (Luke 19:37),
but then it is hidden again for a period. Verse 41 describes the panoramic view of the final descent when the
white, limestone temple comes into full view.

▣ "disciples began to praise God joyfully with a loud voice for all the miracles which they had seen"
"The whole crowd of disciples" refers to

- the disciples (cf. Luke 19:39)

- those who traveled with them

- pilgrims from Galilee who Jesus joined on the way to Jerusalem (cf. Luke 19:39)

"All the miracles which they had seen" refers to Jesus' previous actions from Luke 9:51 through this context,
which happened on the road to Jerusalem.

verses.zh: 说：奉主名来的王是应当称颂的！在天上有和平；在至高之处有荣光。
verses.en: “Blessed is the king[NOTE:1] who comes in the name of the Lord![NOTE:2] Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!”
notes: Luke adds the title king to the citation from Ps 118:26 to make clear who was meant (see Luke 18:38). The psalm was used in looking for the deliverance of the end, thus leading to the Pharisees’ reaction.
A quotation from Ps 118:26.
verses.commentary:
19:38 "Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord" This is a quote
from Ps. 118:26, but is modified:

- "the King" replaces "the one who" (cf. Luke 13:35)

- it omits Mark's "hosanna" (cf. Mark 11:9-10 because Gentiles would not know this term)

This quote (and Mark's) does not fit the MT (Masoretic Text) or the LXX (Septuagint). This is part
of the Hallel (praise) psalms (Psalm 113-118) that were traditionally

- quoted to pilgrims entering Jerusalem during the Passover season

- chanted while the Passover lambs were slaughtered in the temple

- chanted on the first day of Passover (and the other major feast days)

- quoted before meals during Passover week (Psalm 113-114) and after meals (Psalm 115-118)

I believe much that is being said here was done every year, but the fact that the people of Jerusalem
and the pilgrims applied the text specifically to Jesus of Nazareth shows that they understood the uniqueness
of His person and work. This was not just another Passover!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE NAME OF THE LORD

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH

▣ "Peace in heaven and glory in the highest" This phrase is not part of Ps. 118:26. It was part of
the angel's message to the shepherds (cf. Luke 2:14). The promised peace is about to have a surprising redemptive
cost (i.e., Calvary, cf. Isaiah 53 ).

verses.zh: 众人中有几个法利赛人对耶稣说：「夫子，责备你的门徒吧！」
verses.en: But[NOTE:1] some of the Pharisees[NOTE:2] in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast present in this context. Not all present are willing to join in the acclamation.
See the note on Pharisees in 5:17.
Teacher, rebuke your disciples. The Pharisees were complaining that the claims were too great.
verses.commentary:
19:39 "Some of the Pharisees in the crowd said" This refers to

- the Pharisees who welcomed pilgrims to Jerusalem

- the Pharisees who were part of the pilgrims who were traveling from Galilee through the Perean
area to Jerusalem for the Passover Feast

- the Pharisees planted in the crowd trying to find some way to charge Jesus with blasphemy
(cf. Luke 13:31; 14:1,3; 15:2; 16:14; 17:20; 19:39)

Jesus' answer clearly asserts His sense of Messianic fulfillment in this statement (cf. Luke 19:40).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PHARISEES

verses.zh: 耶稣说：「我告诉你们，若是他们闭口不说，这些石头必要呼叫起来。」
verses.en: He answered,[NOTE:1] “I tell you, if they[NOTE:2] keep silent, the very stones[NOTE:3] will cry out!”
notes: Grk “and answering, he said.” This has been simplified in the translation to “He answered.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “these.”
This statement amounts to a rebuke. The idiom of creation speaking means that even creation knows what is taking place, yet the Pharisees miss it. On this idiom, see Gen 4:10 and Hab 2:11.
verses.commentary:
19:40 "if" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE (using ean, cf. Acts 8:31).

▣ "the stones will cry out" This is possibly a proverb of immanent divine judgment (cf. Hab. 2:11).
It could relate to nature's convulsions at God's approach (i.e., visitation, cf. Luke 19:44).

verses.zh: 耶稣快到耶路撒冷，看见城，就为它哀哭，
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] when Jesus[NOTE:2] approached[NOTE:3] and saw the city, he wept over it,
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the transition to a new topic.
Grk “he.”
When Jesus approached and saw the city. This is the last travel note in Luke’s account (the so-called Jerusalem journey), as Jesus approached and saw the city before entering it.
verses.commentary:
19:41 "He saw the city and wept over it" Here we see Jesus expressing human emotions over the tragedy of
His rejection by His own people (cf. Luke 13:34-35). The OT conditional promises have been nullified; only
judgment remains!

verses.zh: 说：「巴不得你在这日子知道关系你平安的事；无奈这事现在是隐藏的，叫你的眼看不出来。
verses.en: saying, “If you had only known on this day,[NOTE:1] even you, the things that make for peace![NOTE:2] But now they are hidden[NOTE:3] from your eyes.
notes: On this day. They had missed the time of Messiah’s coming; see v. 44.
Grk “the things toward peace.” This expression seems to mean “the things that would ‘lead to,’ ‘bring about,’ or ‘make for’ peace.”

But now they are hidden from your eyes. This becomes an oracle of doom in the classic OT sense; see Luke 13:31-35; 11:49-51; Jer 9:2; 13:7; 14:7. They are now blind and under judgment (Jer 15:5; Ps 122:6).
verses.commentary:
19:42 "if" This is an incomplete SECOND CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE (A. T. Robertson,
Word Pictures, vol. 2, p. 246). The Jewish leadership and most of the population of Jerusalem ("even you")
did not know the significance of Jesus' coming.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK GRAMMATICAL TERMS, VII.

NASB, NRSV
"the things which make for peace"

NKJV
"the things that make for your peace"

TEV
"what is needed for peace"

NJB
"the way to peace"

Peshitta
"those who came for your peace"

This is a broken, incomplete sentence. Jesus' emotions over Jerusalem's coming judgment
overwhelms Him! This spiritual peace, peace with God (this is a word play on "Jerusalem," BDB 436, "possession
of peace") comes only through faith in Christ. Jesus brought this peace if they would have only listened to
Him and responded (cf. Isa. 48:18). Jesus was not the kind of Messiah they expected, so they rejected Him
and by so doing, sealed their physical (destruction of Jerusalem) and spiritual (personal and corporate
lostness) doom.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE (NT)

▣ "but now they have been hidden from your eyes" This is an AORIST ACTIVE INDICATIVE.
Luke mentioned this in Luke 9:45; 10:21; 18:34. It either denotes a divine blinding (cf. Rom. 11:7,25 from Deut. 29:4;
Isa. 6:9-10; 29:10) or an idiom expressing rejection.

verses.zh: 因为日子将到，你的仇敌必筑起土垒，周围环绕你，四面困住你，
verses.en: For the days will come upon you when your enemies will build[NOTE:1] an embankment[NOTE:2] against you and surround you and close in on you from every side.
notes: Jesus now predicted the events that would be fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem in a.d. 70. The details of the siege have led some to see Luke writing this after Jerusalem’s fall, but the language of the verse is like God’s exilic judgment for covenant unfaithfulness (Hab 2:8; Jer 6:6, 14; 8:13-22; 9:1; Ezek 4:2; 26:8; Isa 29:1-4). Specific details are lacking and the procedures described (build an embankment against you) were standard Roman military tactics.
An embankment refers to either wooden barricades or earthworks, or a combination of the two.
verses.commentary:
19:43-44 This seems to refer to the destruction of Jerusalem (in five descriptive phrases of OT siege
warfare, cf. Jeremiah 6) under the Roman General Titus in A.D. 70, as well as possibly foreshadowing
the events of eschatological judgment (cf. Luke 21; Psalm 2; Isa. 29:1-4; Ezekiel 38-39; Dan. 9:24-27;
Zechariah 13-14; Rev. 20:7-10).

The Bible is clear that a period of persecution precedes the Second Coming. However, some
commentators believe that A.D.70 completely fulfills this prediction. They are called preterists.
A good example of this position is John Bray, Matthew 24 Fulfilled.

Other commentators expect a future literal fulfillment affecting the city of Jerusalem and the
nation of Israel. They are called dispensational premillennialists. Two good books are Dispensationalism
Today by Charles C. Ryrie (reformed dispensationalism) and Progressive Dispensationalism by
Blaising and Bock (progressive dispensationalism). There are also many who are historical premillennialists,
like George E. Ladd, A Commentary on the Revelation of John, who hold to a similar end-time agenda.

This may be a multiple fulfillment prophecy, but I think the NT universalizes the OT prophecies
whereby geographical and/or racial Israel is no longer the key to the gospel. The OT prophecies have been
fulfilled and now include all people.

19:43 "the days will come" This was an idiom used of

- the eschatological coming of the bridegroom (cf. Luke 5:35)

- the destruction of Jerusalem (cf. Luke 23:29)

This idiom is used in the Septuagint of God's judgment on

- Eli and his family (cf. 1 Sam. 2:31)

- Hezekiah's arrogant actions turning into prophecy of Judah's and the temple's destruction by Babylon
(cf. 2 Kgs. 20:17)

verses.zh: 并要扫灭你和你里头的儿女，连一块石头也不留在石头上，因你不知道眷顾你的时候。」
verses.en: They will demolish you[NOTE:1]—you and your children within your walls[NOTE:2]—and they will not leave within you one stone[NOTE:3] on top of another[NOTE:4] because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God.”[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “They will raze you to the ground.” sn The singular pronoun you refers to the city of Jerusalem personified.
Grk “your children within you.” The phrase “[your] walls” has been supplied in the translation to clarify that the city of Jerusalem, metaphorically pictured as an individual, is spoken of here.
(Not) one stone on top of another is an idiom for total destruction.
Grk “leave stone on stone.”

You did not recognize the time of your visitation refers to the time God came to visit them. They had missed the Messiah; see Luke 1:68-79.tn Grk “the time of your visitation.” To clarify what this refers to, the words “from God” are supplied at the end of the verse, although they do not occur in the Greek text.
verses.commentary:
19:44 "Because you did not recognize" This refers to Luke 19:42 (SECOND CLASS CONDITIONAL
SENTENCE). The Jews should have seen evidence in Jesus' words and actions that fulfilled OT prophecy.
Their cherished traditions blinded them to the truth, however. May God have mercy on all of the fallen race of
Adam!

Although Jesus never specifically mentions "the remnant" concept from the OT prophets, in effect,
His disciples and followers were this believing prophetic remnant from Israel (cf. "little flock" of Luke 12:32).
Even in the OT Israel as a whole was never "right" with YHWH. The "lost" of Luke 19:10 surely includes Israel!

SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (THREE SENSES)

▣ "the time of your visitation" From the OT this time of visitation could be for blessing or judgment
(cf. Isa. 10:3; 23:17; 24:22; 29:6, episkopē in the LXX). In Luke 1:68,78 and 1 Pet. 2:12 it is a
visitation of blessing for believers, but judgment for unbelievers (i.e., the Second Coming). It must be
remembered that God's love and grace spurned turns to God's wrath of accountability and judgment
(cf. the parable of Luke 19:11-27).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

NASB
"and they will level you to the ground and your children within you"

NKJV
"and level you, and your children with you"

NRSV
"they will crush you to the ground, you and your children within you"

TEV
"they will completely destroy you and the people within your walls"

NJB
"they will crush you and the children inside your walls to the ground"

Peshitta
"and will overthrow you and your children within you"

The death of children may be an allusion to Ps. 137:8-9, where the very same VERB
is used in the Septuagint. The VERB literally means "to level" (cf. Isa. 3:26), but came to
mean imagery for "to dash to the ground" (cf. Hos. 10:14; Nah. 3:10). This VERB occurs
only here in the NT. As salvation affected Zaccheus' family (cf. Luke 19:9), so too, is judgment a corporate
experience (i.e., all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, cf. Luke 19:44-45).

I often ponder this corporate aspect of biblical faith, since I have grown up in a western,
individual-focused culture. However, the Bible speaks of judgment to the third and fourth generations
(cf. Deut. 5:9), but covenant loyalty to a thousand generations (cf. Deut. 5:10; 7:9)! This has helped me
in my confidence that God will work with my children and their children (but this does not eliminate personal
choice and consequences).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHRISTIANITY IS CORPORATE

verses.zh: 耶稣进了殿，赶出里头做买卖的人，
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] Jesus[NOTE:2] entered the temple courts[NOTE:3] and began to drive out those who were selling things there,[NOTE:4]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “he.”
The merchants (those who were selling things there) would have been located in the Court of the Gentiles.tn Grk “the temple” (also in v. 47).

Matthew (21:12-27), Mark (11:15-19) and Luke (here, 19:45-46) record this incident of the temple cleansing at the end of Jesus’ ministry. John (2:13-16) records a cleansing of the temple at the beginning of Jesus’ ministry. See the note on the word temple courts in John 2:14 for a discussion of the relationship of these accounts to one another.
verses.commentary:
19:45 "Jesus entered the temple and began to drive out those who were selling" This seems to be a prophetic
fulfillment of Mal. 3:1-2 ("suddenly" is combined with "judgment"). John 2:13ff records a cleansing of the temple
earlier in Jesus' ministry, while the Synoptics record a cleansing in the last week of His ministry. Because
of the thematic organization and freedom of the four Gospel writers, it is uncertain whether there were only
one or two cleansings of the temple. The Sadducees owned the commercial rights on the Mount of Olives and in the
Court of the Gentiles. They were cheating the people

- with their exorbitant charges to exchange common coins into the Tyrian shekel (i.e., the temple accepted only shekels)

- their quick disqualifications of sacrificial animals brought from home

The sacrificial animals available through these merchants were very expensive.

This act of Jesus

- reveals His authority

- reveals the corruption in God's house

- in Luke, written for Gentiles, it symbolized Jesus making room for them again (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:43)

- seals His death by the Jewish leaders (Sadducees, Herodians, and Pharisees, cf. Luke 19:47)

verses.zh: 对他们说：「经上说：我的殿必作祷告的殿，你们倒使它成为贼窝了。」
verses.en: saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house will be a house of prayer,’[NOTE:1] but you have turned it into a den[NOTE:2] of robbers!”[NOTE:3]
notes: A quotation from Isa 56:7.
Or “a hideout” (see L&N 1.57).

A quotation from Jer 7:11. The meaning of Jesus’ statement about making the temple courts a den of robbers probably operates here at two levels. Not only were the religious leaders robbing the people financially, but because of this they had also robbed them spiritually by stealing from them the opportunity to come to know God genuinely. It is possible that these merchants had recently been moved to this location for convenience.
verses.commentary:
19:46 "It is written" This is a Hebrew idiom for Scripture. Exactly why Luke did not quote the entire passage
(cf. Isa. 56:7), which continues (in both MT and LXX), "unto all nations" is uncertain, because it would seem
to fit his recurrent theme of Luke of a universal love of God through Jesus for all humans (of which Zaccheus
is an immediate example).

▣ "but you have made it a robber's den" Jesus is combining Isa. 57:6 with Jer. 7:11 ("a den of robbers").
Jeremiah 7 is the prophet's famous temple sermon addressed to those who are trusting in the temple instead of YHWH.
This combining of texts was a typical rabbinical hermeneutical technique.

SPECIAL TOPIC: RABBINICAL HERMENEUTICAL TECHNIQUES

verses.zh: 耶稣天天在殿里教训人。祭司长和文士与百姓的尊长都想要杀他，
verses.en: Jesus[NOTE:1] was teaching daily in the temple courts. The chief priests and the experts in the law[NOTE:2] and the prominent leaders among the people were seeking to assassinate[NOTE:3] him,
notes: Grk “And he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity. Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “and the scribes.” See the note on the phrase “experts in the law” in 5:21.

Grk “to destroy.”sn The action at the temple was the last straw. In their view, if Jesus could cause trouble in the holy place, then he must be stopped, so the leaders were seeking to assassinate him.
verses.commentary:
19:47 "He was teaching daily in the temple" This is a PERIPHRASTIC IMPERFECT. Jesus
taught regularly in public during this last week of His life. Part of the temple area was dedicated to teaching.
It was known as the Portico of Solomon and it surrounded the Court of the Women, therefore, all visitors to
the temple (Jewish men and women, as well as Gentiles) could hear Him.

▣ This verse is the culmination of the hostility which began in Luke 6:11and 11:53-54. It is quite sad,
the leaders refused to listen to Jesus because they were threatened by His popularity (cf. v. 48). However, His
popularity never lasted because the crowd heard the call to total commitment and service that was required and
they were unwilling to pay the cost. The leaders wanted a different gospel and the people an easier gospel!

verses.zh: 但寻不出法子来，因为百姓都侧耳听他。
verses.en: but[NOTE:1] they could not find a way to do it,[NOTE:2] for all the people hung on his words.[NOTE:3]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast present in this context.
Grk “they did not find the thing that they might do.”
All the people hung on his words is an idiom for intent, eager listening. Jesus’ popularity and support made it unwise for the leadership to seize him.
